title: Rhythm Foundations
goal: Play quarters, eighths, triplets and sixteenths, with rests and off-beats, in time with a click and then with a band.
assumes: You can hold a pick and play a single note on an open string and at a fret. If you have never played at all, do the Beginner Level of First Chords and Strumming first, or alongside this one. You don't need to have used a click before. The minutes listed are one pass through the material; expect to come back to each Step for days.

skills: One clean note at a time

orderRationale: The beat first, then two notes to a beat, then silence, because a rest is harder to place than a note. Off-beats come before sixteenths: they use the same eighth-note count, and a player who can't feel the 'and' will not feel the 'e' or the 'a'. Triplets follow sixteenths so the two ways of dividing a beat can be compared. The Advanced Level mixes them. One riff at the end of the Beginner Level is played with a band, and the band has a Step of its own last, because a band hides a loose rhythm that a click exposes.
gradingLimits: The app times each note you play against where it is written and counts the notes it heard, and in most Exercises it checks after the take that the notes were the written ones. Where a note is written to ring across a bar line, and where two strings are played at once, it times and counts the strokes and does not check which notes they were. It does not grade silence itself: a note played in a rest counts as an extra note, and a string left ringing through a rest is yours to hear. Counting out loud and tapping your foot are taught here and not checked. Your setup adds a small delay between playing and the app hearing it, which matters little at these tempos. None of this has been tried on a real guitar yet.

steps.title: On the beat
steps.goal: Play one note on every click, and hold a note for two clicks or four, without drifting.
steps.why: Everything in music hangs on the beat. Playing exactly with a click feels strange at first: when you are right on it, the click seems to disappear behind your note. That feeling is the thing to learn, and it is easiest to find with one slow note at a time.
howTo: The words this Path uses. The strings, from thickest to thinnest: low E, A, D, G, B and the top string. Fret 1 is the first space next to the nut, at the head end of the neck. Fingers are numbered from the index finger: first, second, third, and the little finger is the fourth.

A click is the tick of the metronome. Each tick is a beat, four beats make a bar, and BPM is how many beats go by in a minute. A whole note lasts a whole bar, a half note two beats, a quarter note one beat. The pass tempo is the speed at which an Exercise counts as done.

One play through an Exercise is a Take. Each Exercise has a ladder of tempos called rungs: between Takes, Slower and Faster move one rung along it, and the pass tempo is the rung at which the Exercise counts as done. Some Exercises change key or string from Take to Take.
On the tab each line is a string: the top line is the top string and the bottom line is the low E string. Each number is the fret to press. 0 is an open string, one played with no finger on it.
Count '1, 2, 3, 4' out loud with the click before you play, and keep counting while you play.
Every note is a downstroke. Let the pick fall through the string and rest against the next one.
A half note lasts two clicks and a whole note four. Let it ring for its full length and count through it.
steps.payoff: A four-bar riff on two strings that lands on every click.

exercises.title: One note a click
exercises.purpose: Open strings only, one note on each click, then two long notes to finish. The fretting hand does nothing, so all of your attention is on the beat.
howTo: Quarter notes: four on the lower string, four on the upper, two and two, then a half note on each.
Listen for the click vanishing under your note. If you hear the click just before or after you, you are late or early.
exercises.coachLine: I time each note against the click and say how even they were. Counting out loud is yours to keep going.

cues.say: Play so the click vanishes under each note.
Strike every note, one on each click.
Pick one note on each click, no more.
Play each note right with the click.
Wait for the click before each note.
Count the long note out, then come in.
Rest the fretting hand and count the beats.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Hold each long note for two full clicks.

selfCheck: Could you count the beats out loud while you played it?

exercises.title: Long notes and short ones
exercises.purpose: A half note, then two quarters, and a whole note to end. Holding a note for exactly two clicks is harder than playing two notes.
howTo: Count '1, 2' through each half note and play the quarters on 3 and 4. The last bar is one note held for all four clicks.
On the low E string the fretted note is at fret 3. On the A string it is at fret 2. Third finger for fret 3, second finger for fret 2.
exercises.coachLine: I time when each note starts. How long you let it ring is for your ear and your count.

cues.say: Count '1, 2' right through each long note.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Let the long note ring; don't pick it again.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Play the notes on '3' and '4' with the click.
Wait for '3' before you play again.
Count the long note out, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Find the next string during the long note.
Hold the last note for all four clicks.

selfCheck: Did each long note ring until the next note started?

variants.label: A and D strings
howTo: Count '1, 2' through each half note and play the quarters on 3 and 4. The last bar is one note held for all four clicks.
On the A and D strings the fretted note is at fret 2.

variants.label: D and G strings
howTo: Count '1, 2' through each half note and play the quarters on 3 and 4. The last bar is one note held for all four clicks.
On the D and G strings the fretted note is at fret 2.

exercises.title: A riff in quarter notes
exercises.purpose: E minor pentatonic is a scale of five notes that sound good together, and a riff is a short phrase that repeats. This riff plays four of the five on two strings, a note on every click for three bars and two half notes to end. Your first riff with a click.
howTo: Open string, fretted note, open string, fretted note. Keep the fretting fingers close to the strings so they are ready.
All downstrokes. If a note is late, it is nearly always the fretting finger arriving late, not the pick.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

cues.say: Keep the fretting fingers close to the strings.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Pick one note on each click, no more.
Say 'open, fret, open, fret' as you play.
Have the finger down before its click.
Wait for the click before each note.
Count the long note out, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Hold each of the last two notes for two clicks.

steps.title: Two to a beat
steps.goal: Play eighth notes, two to every click, down on the beat and up on the 'and', and change between quarters and eighths without a bump.
steps.why: Eighth notes are where the picking hand starts to swing like a pendulum: down on the beat, up between beats. That motion is the clock for every rhythm after this one. If the up note is early or quiet, the line limps.
howTo: Count '1 and 2 and 3 and 4 and'. Downstroke on the numbers, upstroke on every 'and'.
Make the upstroke as loud as the downstroke. It is usually quieter because the pick catches less string.
When the rhythm goes back to quarter notes, the hand keeps swinging and simply misses the string on the way up.
steps.payoff: A riff in eighths that drives, and long, short-short, the commonest rhythm in rock.

exercises.title: Quarters, then eighths
exercises.purpose: One bar with a note on each click, then the same notes twice as fast. The click does not change; you fit two notes into it.
howTo: Bar 1: four quarter notes, all down. Bar 2: each note twice, down then up.
The first note of bar 2 lands exactly on the click, like every note in bar 1 did.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even each bar was. The join between the bars is usually where the time slips.

cues.say: Fit two notes into each click, down then up.
Pick both notes of each pair, down and up.
Pick each note twice in bar two, not more.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Put the first note of bar two on the click.
Wait for the click before bar two starts.
Let each quarter note last its whole click.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Keep the down-up going to the last note.

exercises.title: A riff in eighths
exercises.purpose: Two bars of steady eighths in E minor pentatonic with a long note to end. The pick never stops: down, up, down, up.
howTo: Strictly down on the beat and up on the 'and', even when the string changes.
Tap your foot on the click. The foot goes down with every downstroke.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones. The direction of each stroke is yours to keep.

cues.say: Down on the beat, up on the 'and'.
Pick every note, down and up alike.
Keep the pick on the two strings in use.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Put each downstroke on the foot's tap.
Wait for the foot's tap on each downstroke.
Count the last note's beat, then start again.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Stay down-up as you change string.
Keep the pick going down-up to the end.

exercises.title: Long, short-short
exercises.purpose: A quarter note and two eighths, over and over: the commonest rhythm in rock. The hand swings in eighths the whole time and skips one upstroke.
howTo: Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and'. Down on 1, then down-up on '2 and'.
On the quarter note the hand still comes up; it just passes over the string without touching it.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

cues.say: Keep the hand swinging through the long note.
Pick both short notes of each pair.
Let the upstroke miss on each long note.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Put each long note right on the click.
Wait for the click on each long note.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and' to the last note.

steps.title: Silence in time
steps.goal: Stop the strings on the beat and come back in on the beat, so a rest is as exact as a note.
steps.why: A rest is not a pause; it is a note of silence with a start and an end. Most beginners rush through rests because nothing is happening. Riffs get their punch from the stops, and a stop only works if it is in time.
howTo: To stop an open string, lay the side of the picking hand on the strings at the bridge. To stop a fretted note, relax the finger without lifting it off the string.
Keep counting through the rest, out loud, and keep the foot tapping.
The picking hand keeps its swing through a rest and plays the air.
steps.payoff: A riff that stops dead and comes back in, exactly together with the click.

exercises.title: Play one, rest one
exercises.purpose: A note on a click, silence on the next; bar 3 moves the rest to beat 3. The last bar is one note and three beats of nothing, which is longer than it sounds.
howTo: Play on the click, then stop the string exactly on the next click. Count the rests as loudly as the notes.
In bar 4, play on beat 1 and count '2, 3, 4' in silence before the loop starts again.
exercises.coachLine: I time the notes. A note played in a rest counts as an extra note; a string left ringing is for your ear.

cues.say: Count the rests as loudly as the notes.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick off the strings in the rests.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Play right on the click after each rest.
Count the rest out loud before you come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move to the next string during the rest.
Count '2, 3, 4' out loud in the last rests.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

exercises.title: Run and stop
exercises.purpose: Four eighths, a quarter note, and a beat of silence. The stop on beat 4 is what makes it a riff.
howTo: Count '1 and 2 and 3, (4)'. A number in brackets is a beat you count and do not play. Stop the string on 4 and come back in on the next 1.
Don't speed up into the stop. The four eighths are the same speed as always.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take. The silence on beat 4 is yours to keep clean.

cues.say: Stop the string on '4', come in on '1'.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick off the strings on '4'.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Come in right on the '1' after the stop.
Keep the eighths steady going into the stop.
Count '(4)' in silence, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count the last '(4)' before starting again.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

exercises.title: A question and an answer
exercises.purpose: Two short phrases with silence after each, the second with two beats of rest. The rests are where the other player would answer.
howTo: Bar 1: quarter, two eighths, quarter, rest. Bar 2: two eighths, quarter, then two beats of rest.
Hear the phrase echo in your head during the rest. That keeps the count going without thinking about it.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

cues.say: Echo the phrase in your head during the rest.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick off the strings in the rests.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Play right on the click after each rest.
Count the rest out loud before you come in.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count both beats of the last rest.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

exercises.title: Two beats on, two beats off
exercises.purpose: Four eighths and then half a bar of silence. Coming back in after two empty beats is the test of whether you are still counting.
howTo: Count '1 and 2 and, 3, 4'. Beats 3 and 4 are silent every bar.
Breathe out in the rest. A tense hand comes back in early.
exercises.coachLine: The first note after each rest is the one I'd look at: early is the usual mistake.

cues.say: Count '3, 4' in silence, then come in on '1'.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick off the strings in the rests.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Play right on the click after each rest.
Breathe out through both silent beats.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move to the next string during the rest.
Count the last two silent beats out loud.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

steps.difficultyException: Fewer notes a bar than the Step before, on purpose: placing silence and coming back in on time is the demand, and a note-rate metric does not count it.

steps.title: The same rhythms on other strings
steps.goal: Play quarters, eighths and rests on the D and G strings and on the G and B strings, then a tune at the fifth fret and one riff that crosses three strings with a band, as steadily as on the low strings.
steps.why: Nearly everything so far has been written on the two lowest strings. The rhythms do not belong to those strings: the count, the foot and the swing of the picking hand are the same anywhere on the guitar. What changes is the feel under the pick. The higher strings are thinner and give way more easily, so it is easy to hit them too hard and to rush. Nothing in the rhythm is new here, on purpose.
howTo: The same five notes carry on across the strings. On the D and G strings the fretted note is at fret 2, under the second finger. On the B and top E strings it is at fret 3, under the third finger.
Count out loud before you play, as in the Steps before: '1, 2, 3, 4' for quarter notes and '1 and 2 and' for eighths. Down on the beat, up on the 'and'.
Use a lighter stroke than on the low E string, keep the foot tapping, and count through every rest.
For the tune at the fifth fret the hand moves up the neck. That Exercise names its own frets and fingers.
The last Exercise is played with a band. Listen to the bass drum and the snare, not to your own guitar.
steps.payoff: A tune at the fifth fret, and a four-bar riff across the D, G and B strings with quarters, eighths and a rest in it, played with a band for the first time.

exercises.title: Quarters and eighths, higher up
exercises.purpose: A two-bar riff on the D and G strings: quarter notes, a pair of eighths, a run of four eighths and a half note to end. The rhythms are the ones you already know; only the strings are new.
howTo: Count '1, 2, 3 and, 4', then '1 and 2 and, 3, 4'. The note on 3 is a half note: let it ring while you say 4.
Bar 1: the open D string, E at fret 2, the open G string twice, A at fret 2. Bar 2: the open G string, A, the open G string, the open D string, then E held.
Down on every beat, up on each 'and'. One finger to a fret, as before: the second finger at fret 2.
exercises.coachLine: Timing against the click, and the right notes after the take. Counting out loud is yours to keep going.

cues.say: Let the half note ring while you say '4'.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick on the two strings in use.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note out, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Hold the last note while you count '3, 4'.

selfCheck: Could you count the beats out loud while you played it?

variants.label: B and top E strings
variants.purpose: A two-bar riff on the B and top E strings: quarter notes, a pair of eighths, a run of four eighths and a half note to end. The rhythms are the ones you already know; only the strings are new.
howTo: Count '1, 2, 3 and, 4', then '1 and 2 and, 3, 4'. The note on 3 is a half note: let it ring while you say 4.
Bar 1: the open B string, D at fret 3, the open top string twice, G at fret 3. Bar 2: the open top string, G, the open top string, the open B string, then D held.
Down on every beat, up on each 'and'.

exercises.title: Long and short, higher up
exercises.purpose: Long, short-short and a run of eighths on the G and B strings. The fretted note on the G string is at fret 2. On the B string it is at fret 3.
howTo: Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and', then '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.

Bar 1: the open G string, A at fret 2, the open B string. Then D at fret 3 on the B string, the open B string, and A again. Bar 2: the open G string twice, A, the open G string, the open B string, D, and the open B string on beat 4.
On each quarter note the hand still swings up and passes over the string without touching it. Second finger at fret 2, third finger at fret 3.
exercises.coachLine: Timing against the click, and the right notes after the take. Keeping each upstroke as loud as the downstroke before it is yours to hear.

cues.say: Swing up past the string on each quarter.
Pick each upstroke as firmly as the down.
Keep the pick on the two strings in use.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count '3 and, 4' and land the last note.

variants.label: D and G strings
variants.purpose: Long, short-short and a run of eighths on the D and G strings. The fretted note on the D string is at fret 2. On the G string it is at fret 2.
howTo: Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and', then '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.

Bar 1: the open D string, E at fret 2, the open G string. Then A at fret 2 on the G string, the open G string, and E again. Bar 2: the open D string twice, E, the open D string, the open G string, A, and the open G string on beat 4.
On each quarter note the hand still swings up and passes over the string without touching it.

variants.label: B and top E strings
variants.purpose: Long, short-short and a run of eighths on the B and top E strings. The fretted note on the B string is at fret 3. On the top string it is at fret 3.
howTo: Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and', then '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.

Bar 1: the open B string, D at fret 3, the open top string. Then G at fret 3 on the top string, the open top string, and D again. Bar 2: the open B string twice, D, the open B string, the open top string, G, and the open top string on beat 4.
On each quarter note the hand still swings up and passes over the string without touching it.

exercises.title: Stops, higher up
exercises.purpose: Two bars on the D and G strings with one beat of silence in each: beat 2 of the first bar and beat 3 of the second. The rest moves, so it has to be counted.
howTo: Count '1, (2), 3 and, 4', then '1 and, 2, (3), 4'. Say the rests as loudly as the notes.
Bar 1: E at fret 2 on the D string, a rest, the open D string twice, the open G string. Bar 2: A at fret 2 on the G string, the open G string, E, a rest, the open D string.

Both rests come straight after the E, a fretted note. Relax the fretting finger without lifting it off the string, and lay the side of the picking hand on the strings to stop any open string that is still ringing.
exercises.coachLine: The notes are timed and checked after the take. A note played in a rest counts as an extra note; a string left ringing is for your ear.

cues.say: Say each rest as loudly as the notes.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick off the strings in the rests.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Play right on the click after each rest.
Count the rest out loud before you come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count '(3)' in silence, then play '4'.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

variants.label: B and top E strings
variants.purpose: Two bars on the B and top E strings with one beat of silence in each: beat 2 of the first bar and beat 3 of the second. The rest moves, so it has to be counted.
howTo: Count '1, (2), 3 and, 4', then '1 and, 2, (3), 4'. Say the rests as loudly as the notes.
Bar 1: D at fret 3 on the B string, a rest, the open B string twice, the open top string. Bar 2: G at fret 3 on the top string, the open top string, D, a rest, the open B string.

Both rests come straight after the D, a fretted note. Relax the fretting finger without lifting it off the string, and lay the side of the picking hand on the strings to stop any open string that is still ringing.

exercises.title: A tune at the fifth fret
exercises.purpose: The same rhythms higher up the neck: a short melody on the G and B strings with the hand at the fifth fret, eighths and quarters, ending on a long note. These four notes come back later in the Path.
howTo: On the G string, first finger at fret 5 and third finger at fret 7. On the B string, first finger at fret 5 and little finger at fret 8. Find the notes slowly without the click first.
Count it first without the guitar: '1 and 2, 3 and 4', then '1 and 2 and 3' and hold. Then play what you counted.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

cues.say: Count it once without the guitar, then play.
Press each finger right behind the fret.
Keep the pick on the G and B strings.
Use one finger per fret: five, seven, eight.
Put the first note of each beat on the click.
Wait for the click at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Have the next finger ready as you cross.
Hold the last note for both beats.

exercises.title: A riff across three strings
exercises.purpose: Four bars on the D, G and B strings, each bar with its own rhythm from earlier in the Level: quarters with a pair of eighths, a run that stops, long short-short, and a mix to finish.
howTo: The band is a drummer and a bassist in place of the click.
If you get lost, stop, find beat 1 of the next bar and come back in there.
Count each bar before you play it: '1, 2, 3 and, 4', then '1 and 2 and, 3, (4)', then '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and', then '1 and, 2, 3 and, 4'.

Bar 1 climbs: the open D string, E at fret 2, the open G string, A at fret 2, the open B string. Bar 2 starts on the B string, on D at fret 3. Then it comes down: the open B string, A, the open G string, E on beat 3, and a rest on beat 4.

Bar 3 climbs again: the open D string, E at fret 2 twice, the open G string, A at fret 2 twice. Bar 4 comes back down: the open B string, D at fret 3, the open B string. Then A, the open G string, and E on beat 4.
Second finger at fret 2, third finger at fret 3. The hand does not move.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece, with the band on. Timing against the band, and the right notes after the take.

cues.say: Count each bar out loud before you play it.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Keep the pick on the three strings in use.
Read one note ahead in the tab as you play.
Land each bar's first note with the band.
Wait for the band at the start of each beat.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Lift the finger off in time for open notes.
Move the pick across during the note before.
Count the last bar out loud as you play it.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

selfCheck: Could you count the beats out loud while you played it?

variants.label: A, D and G strings
variants.purpose: Four bars on the A, D and G strings, each bar with its own rhythm from earlier in the Level: quarters with a pair of eighths, a run that stops, long short-short, and a mix to finish.
howTo: The band is a drummer and a bassist in place of the click.
If you get lost, stop, find beat 1 of the next bar and come back in there.
Count each bar before you play it: '1, 2, 3 and, 4', then '1 and 2 and, 3, (4)', then '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and', then '1 and, 2, 3 and, 4'.

Bar 1 climbs: the open A string, B at fret 2, the open D string, E at fret 2, the open G string. Bar 2 starts on the G string, on A at fret 2. Then it comes down: the open G string, E, the open D string, B on beat 3, and a rest on beat 4.

Bar 3 climbs again: the open A string, B at fret 2 twice, the open D string, E at fret 2 twice. Bar 4 comes back down: the open G string, A at fret 2, the open G string. Then E, the open D string, and B on beat 4.

steps.title: Between the beats
steps.goal: Play notes on the 'and' with nothing on the beat before them, and hold a note across a beat, while the foot keeps the pulse.
steps.why: Syncopation is a note where the beat is not. It is what makes a rhythm lean forward. The trap is that the off-beat note turns into the beat in your head and you flip the rhythm over; the foot and the pendulum of the hand are what stop that.
howTo: The hand never stops swinging in eighths: down on every beat, up on every 'and'. An off-beat note is always an upstroke.
Where the beat itself is silent, the downstroke plays the air and the foot plays the beat.
A dotted quarter note lasts a beat and a half: count '1 and 2' and play the next note on the 'and' of 2.
steps.payoff: A syncopated riff that pushes against the click and never turns around.

exercises.title: Only the 'and'
exercises.purpose: After the first beat, every note is on an 'and': the beats themselves are silent. The foot has to be the beat, because the guitar no longer is.
howTo: Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and, (4) and'. Play the 'and' with an upstroke and miss the string on the way down.
Tap the foot on every click. The note comes when the foot is in the air.
exercises.coachLine: I time each note against where it is written. Whether your foot kept the beat is yours to say.
selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: A beat and a half
exercises.purpose: A dotted quarter note and an eighth: long, short, long, short. The short note falls on the 'and' of 2 and of 4.
howTo: Count '1 and 2 AND 3 and 4 AND', playing on 1, on the 'and' of 2, on 3 and on the 'and' of 4. In bar 2 the note on 3 is held to the end of the bar.
The long note is a downstroke and the short one an upstroke. Let the long note ring until the short one starts.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

exercises.title: Three, three, two
exercises.purpose: Eight eighths grouped 3 + 3 + 2: three notes a bar, the second one off the beat. It is the rhythm under a great many rock, pop and Latin songs.
howTo: Count the eighths '1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2' and play on every '1'. Then count it as '1, the and of 2, 4' against the click.
Down, up, down. The middle note is the off-beat one.
exercises.coachLine: The second note of each bar is the one that drifts onto the beat. I'll say how even it was.
selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: A syncopated riff
exercises.purpose: Two bars in E minor pentatonic where beats 2 and 3 are silent and the notes around them fall on the 'and'.
howTo: Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and 4'. The hand swings in eighths throughout and plays only the written ones.
Learn it at the first rung with the count out loud. It will feel wrong until it suddenly feels right.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.
selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

steps.difficultyException: Fewer notes a bar than the Step before, on purpose: placing a note on the 'and' with nothing on the beat before it is the demand, and a note-rate metric does not count it.

steps.title: The push
steps.goal: Play a note on the 'and' and let it ring through the next beat, inside a bar and across a bar line, the line between two bars, while the foot taps that beat alone.
steps.why: A push is a note that arrives half a beat early. It belongs to the beat after it: the note for beat 1 is played on the 'and' of 4 and held, so nothing is struck on beat 1 at all. It makes a riff lean into the next bar. You have played notes on the 'and', and you have held a note across a beat; a push is both at once. You have played one already: the middle note of three, three, two. The place it goes wrong is the beat that is not played: with no stroke on it the count slips, and the next note comes early.
howTo: A pushed note is on an 'and', so it is an upstroke. On the beat after it the downstroke plays the air, the foot taps, and the note keeps ringing.

Count the held beat in brackets and still say it: '4 and, (1), 2'. Until now a beat in brackets was silent. In this Step it is a beat with no stroke while a note rings, so don't stop the string on it.

This tab cannot join two notes across a bar line. A push into the next bar is written as a note on the 'and' of 4 marked let ring, with a rest on beat 1 after it. Play it as one long note: that rest is the note still ringing, not silence.
steps.payoff: A four-bar riff that leans into its second and fourth bars, with the foot steady under every push.

exercises.title: A push inside the bar
exercises.purpose: A note on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3: the push in its smallest form. Beat 3 is not played; the note before it is still ringing.
howTo: Count '1, 2 AND, (3), 4'. Down on 1 and on 2, up on the 'and' of 2, miss the string on 3, down on 4.

Bar 1: the open low E string, G at fret 3, then the open A string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3. B at fret 2 on the A string is on beat 4. Bar 2: the open A string, the open low E string, then G pushed and held through beat 3, and the open A string on beat 4.
Tap the foot on beat 3 while the pushed note rings. In bar 2 the pushed note is a fretted one: keep the finger down on it through the beat.
exercises.coachLine: The note on the 'and' of 2 is the one that drifts onto beat 3. Timing against the click, and the right notes after the take.
selfCheck: Did each pushed note ring through the beat after it, while your foot tapped that beat?

variants.label: A and D strings
howTo: Count '1, 2 AND, (3), 4'. Down on 1 and on 2, up on the 'and' of 2, miss the string on 3, down on 4.

Bar 1: the open A string, B at fret 2, then the open D string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3. E at fret 2 on the D string is on beat 4. Bar 2: the open D string, the open A string, then B pushed and held through beat 3, and the open D string on beat 4.
Tap the foot on beat 3 while the pushed note rings. In bar 2 the pushed note is a fretted one: keep the finger down on it through the beat.

variants.label: D and G strings
howTo: Count '1, 2 AND, (3), 4'. Down on 1 and on 2, up on the 'and' of 2, miss the string on 3, down on 4.

Bar 1: the open D string, E at fret 2, then the open G string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3. A at fret 2 on the G string is on beat 4. Bar 2: the open G string, the open D string, then E pushed and held through beat 3, and the open G string on beat 4.
Tap the foot on beat 3 while the pushed note rings. In bar 2 the pushed note is a fretted one: keep the finger down on it through the beat.

exercises.title: A push across the bar line
exercises.purpose: The note for beat 1 of bar 2 comes half a beat early, on the 'and' of 4, and rings across the bar line. Nothing is played on that beat 1.
howTo: Count '1, 2, 3, 4 AND, (1), 2, 3, 4'. The 'and' of 4 is an upstroke; on the next beat 1 the hand comes down past the string and the foot taps alone.

Bar 1: the open low E string, G at fret 3, the open A string. Then B at fret 2 on the A string on beat 4, and the open A string again on the 'and' of 4. That last note rings through beat 1 of bar 2. Beats 2, 3 and 4 of bar 2 are B, the open A string and G.
The rest written on beat 1 of bar 2 is the pushed note carrying on. Don't stop the string there.
exercises.coachLine: The first note after the push, on beat 2, is where the time slips: early is the usual mistake. Each note is timed against the click; which note it was is not checked here. Whether the pushed note rang on is yours to hear.

notes: Notes that ring together are hard to separate: the note checks may give up, and the app says so rather than guessing.

howTo: Count '1, 2, 3, 4 AND, (1), 2, 3, 4'. The 'and' of 4 is an upstroke; on the next beat 1 the hand comes down past the string and the foot taps alone.
Bar 1: the open A string, B at fret 2, the open D string. Then E at fret 2 on the D string on beat 4, and the open D string again on the 'and' of 4. That last note rings through beat 1 of bar 2.
The rest written on beat 1 of bar 2 is the pushed note carrying on. Don't stop the string there.

variants.label: D and G strings
howTo: Count '1, 2, 3, 4 AND, (1), 2, 3, 4'. The 'and' of 4 is an upstroke; on the next beat 1 the hand comes down past the string and the foot taps alone.
Bar 1: the open D string, E at fret 2, the open G string. Then A at fret 2 on the G string on beat 4, and the open G string again on the 'and' of 4. That last note rings through beat 1 of bar 2.
The rest written on beat 1 of bar 2 is the pushed note carrying on. Don't stop the string there.

exercises.title: Both pushes, one after the other
exercises.purpose: A push across the bar line and, straight after it, a push inside the bar. In bar 2 neither beat 1 nor beat 3 is played: each has a note ringing through it.
howTo: Bar 1: the open low E string, G at fret 3 twice, the open A string on beat 3 and again on beat 4. Then B at fret 2 on the A string on the 'and' of 4. Keep the finger down on the B: it rings through beat 1 of bar 2.
Bar 2: the open A string on beat 2, G at fret 3 on the low E string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3, and the open A string again on beat 4.
Both pushed notes are upstrokes. The foot taps every beat, and the two beats with no stroke are the ones to listen for.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.
exercises.coachLine: Each note is timed against the click; which note it was is not checked here. Whether the pushed notes rang on is yours to hear.

Bar 2: the open D string on beat 2, B at fret 2 on the A string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3, and the open D string again on beat 4.
Both pushed notes are upstrokes. The foot taps every beat, and the two beats with no stroke are the ones to listen for.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.

Bar 2: the open G string on beat 2, E at fret 2 on the D string on the 'and' of 2, held through beat 3, and the open G string again on beat 4.
Both pushed notes are upstrokes. The foot taps every beat, and the two beats with no stroke are the ones to listen for.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.

exercises.title: A riff with pushes
exercises.purpose: Four bars on two strings. Bars 1 and 3 run in eighths and end with a push into the next bar; bar 4 answers with a push inside the bar.
howTo: Bars 1 and 3: count '1 and 2 and, 3, 4 AND'. Bar 2: '(1), 2 and, 3, 4'. Bar 4: '(1), 2 AND, (3), 4'.
The push into bar 2 is the open A string. The push into bar 4 is G at fret 3 on the low E string: keep the finger down through beat 1.
In bar 4 the open low E string is on beat 2, the open A string on the 'and' of 2 is held through beat 3, and B at fret 2 on the A string ends the riff on beat 4.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.
The hand swings in eighths from start to finish. Learn it at the first rung with the count out loud.

The push into bar 2 is the open D string. The push into bar 4 is B at fret 2 on the A string: keep the finger down through beat 1.
In bar 4 the open A string is on beat 2, the open D string on the 'and' of 2 is held through beat 3, and E at fret 2 on the D string ends the riff on beat 4.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.
The hand swings in eighths from start to finish. Learn it at the first rung with the count out loud.

The push into bar 2 is the open G string. The push into bar 4 is E at fret 2 on the D string: keep the finger down through beat 1.
In bar 4 the open D string is on beat 2, the open G string on the 'and' of 2 is held through beat 3, and A at fret 2 on the G string ends the riff on beat 4.
The rest written on beat 1 after a push is the pushed note still ringing. Don't stop the string there.
The hand swings in eighths from start to finish. Learn it at the first rung with the count out loud.

steps.title: Four to a beat
steps.goal: Play sixteenth notes and the two figures built from them, long-short-short and short-short-long, evenly with a click.
steps.why: Sixteenths divide the beat in four, and nearly every busy rhythm is a pattern of which of the four you play. The pendulum doubles: the hand now swings four times a beat, and each figure is that swing with one stroke missing.
howTo: Count '1 e and a, 2 e and a'. The hand goes down on the number and the 'and', up on the 'e' and the 'a'.
Long-short-short is '1, and a': down, down-up. It is the quarter and two eighths of the Beginner Level at twice the speed, and it is called the gallop. Short-short-long is '1 e and': down-up, down.
Keep the strokes small. The wrist moves, not the arm.
steps.payoff: A riff with the gallop in it, steady at a tempo where it starts to sound like a band.

exercises.title: Four fast, one slow
exercises.purpose: A beat of sixteenths and then a quarter note to breathe. Four even notes inside one click is the whole skill, in its smallest form.
howTo: Count '1 e and a, 2'. Down, up, down, up, then a downstroke on beat 2.
The four notes fill the beat exactly. If you arrive at beat 2 early, they were rushed.
exercises.coachLine: The quarter note after each group tells me whether the four before it were rushed. I'll say how even it was.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The gallop figure
exercises.purpose: An eighth and two sixteenths on every beat: '1, and a'. A horse's gallop, and the rhythm of a thousand rock riffs.
howTo: Down, down-up on each beat. The hand swings in sixteenths and misses the string on the 'e'.
Keep the two short notes light and even. The long note on the beat is the strong one.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take. Which strokes you used is yours to keep.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The gallop, turned round
exercises.purpose: Two sixteenths and an eighth on every beat: '1 e and'. The same three notes with the short ones first, and it feels completely different.
howTo: Down-up, down on each beat. The hand misses the string on the 'a'.
The first of the two short notes is on the click. Don't let the pair fall early, before the beat.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A riff with both figures
exercises.purpose: Two bars that use the gallop, its reverse, plain eighths and a long note, so you have to change figure on the move.
howTo: Clap or count the rhythm before you play it: '1, and a, 2 e and, 3, and a, 4'.
The hand swings in sixteenths from start to finish. Only which strokes touch the string changes.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

steps.title: Three to a beat
steps.goal: Play eighth-note triplets evenly, change between two and three notes to a beat, and play a shuffle.
steps.why: A triplet divides the beat in three, and it is the first rhythm that will not fit the 'down on the beat' rule: with strict down-up strokes, every other beat starts on an upstroke. The shuffle, the rhythm of blues and a lot of rock, is a triplet with its middle note left out.
howTo: Count '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let'. Three even notes a click, with the first one on it.
Keep strict down-up: beat 1 starts down, beat 2 starts up. Give the first note of each beat a small accent so both sound the same.
A shuffle is long-short, long-short: play the first and third notes of each triplet. Count '1 (trip) let, 2 (trip) let'.
steps.payoff: A boogie shuffle on two strings that rolls along with the click.

exercises.title: Three even notes a click
exercises.purpose: Each note three times, as a triplet: four beats, twelve notes. Getting three to sound even, and not like two fast and one slow, is the point.
howTo: Say '1-trip-let' along with the click before you play. All three syllables the same length.
Strict down-up. The first note of beats 2 and 4 is an upstroke; lean on it a little.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even the triplets were and check the notes after the take.

exercises.title: Two, then three
exercises.purpose: A beat of two eighths, then a beat of three triplets, and again. The click stays where it is and the division changes under it.
howTo: Count '1 and, 2-trip-let, 3 and, 4-trip-let'. The first note of every beat is on the click whichever it is.
The triplet is three even notes, not two eighths with a third squeezed in. Speed the hand up a little less than you think.
exercises.coachLine: The first note after each change is where the time moves. I'll say how even it was.

exercises.title: The shuffle
exercises.purpose: A boogie line on the A and D strings in shuffle rhythm: long-short, long-short, the first and last notes of each triplet.
howTo: Open A string twice, then the D string at fret 2 twice, fret 4 twice, fret 2 twice. First finger on fret 2, third finger on fret 4.
Down on the long note, up on the short one. The short note comes late, just before the next beat, and leads into it.
exercises.coachLine: I time the long and the short notes against the triplet they are written on, so straight eighths will read as early.

exercises.title: A tune in triplets
exercises.purpose: A falling A minor pentatonic phrase in triplets at the fifth fret, with a rest in the first bar and a long note at the end.
howTo: Two beats of triplets, a quarter note, a rest. Then two beats of triplets and a held note.
Six notes in a row cross three strings. Keep the strokes strictly down-up through the crossings.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I'll say how even it was and whether the notes were the written ones.

steps.difficultyException: Three to a beat is fewer notes a second than the sixteenths before it. The new demands are a division that does not line up with the strokes, and the change between two and three, which a note-rate metric does not count.

steps.title: Sixteenths with holes in them
steps.goal: Play sixteenth-note rhythms with rests on the beat and notes on the 'e' and the 'a', and keep the pulse.
steps.why: Funk, and most modern rhythm playing, is sixteenths with some of them left out. The notes that are missing matter as much as the ones that are there, and the hardest note to place is the one right after a silent beat.
howTo: The hand swings in sixteenths all the time, lightly, and only digs in on the written notes.
Count every '1 e and a' out loud at the first rung, and say the played syllables louder.
Stop each note with the fretting hand or the palm so the rests are really silent. Short notes make the rhythm clear.
steps.payoff: A two-bar funk line at the fifth fret that sits in the gaps.

exercises.title: One, e, (and), a
exercises.purpose: Three of the four sixteenths, with the 'and' left out: a skipping figure on each beat, and a quarter note to finish the bar.
howTo: Count '1 e (and) a'. Down, up, miss, up.
The hole is in the middle of the beat. Don't close it up: the 'a' comes late, just before the next beat.
exercises.coachLine: I time each note against where it is written, so a closed-up gap shows as early notes.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Silent on the beat
exercises.purpose: A quarter note, then a beat that starts with silence and plays its 'e', 'and' and 'a'. Coming in just after the click is the skill.
howTo: Count '1, (2) e and a, 3, (4) e and a'. On beats 2 and 4 the downstroke plays the air and the next upstroke starts the group.
Let the foot hit the floor in the hole. The first note comes straight after it.
exercises.coachLine: The first note after each silent beat is the one I'd look at. Early means the rest was cut short.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: Threes across the beat
exercises.purpose: Four notes, each three sixteenths long, then a quarter note. The notes drift off the beat one sixteenth at a time and the quarter brings you home.
howTo: Count sixteenths in threes: '1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3, 1 2 3 4'. Then feel it against the foot on the click.
The notes land on 1, the 'a' of 1, the 'and' of 2, and the 'e' of 3. The quarter note is on beat 4.
exercises.coachLine: Only the first and last notes of the bar are on a beat. I'll say how even the ones between were.
selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: A funk line
exercises.purpose: Two bars of A minor pentatonic on the low strings at the fifth fret, mostly single sixteenths with space around them.
howTo: Learn it a beat at a time: '1, a', then 'e and' of 2, then '3, and', then '4 e'. Bar 2 is the same until beat 3.
Play every note short. Relax the fretting finger straight after each one so it stops.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

steps.difficultyException: The rests bring the note count down. The demand is placing single sixteenths around silent beats, which a note-rate metric does not count.

steps.title: Changing gear
steps.goal: Move between eighths, triplets and sixteenths inside one bar without the beat moving.
steps.why: Real lines change subdivision all the time, and the change is where players speed up or slow down. Going from two to three to four notes a beat, and back, with the first note of every beat on the click, is the best single test of time there is.
howTo: The beat is the only thing that stays the same. Tap it with the foot and fit two, three or four notes inside each tap.
Say the counts in a row before you play: '1 and, 2-trip-let, 3 e and a, 4'.
Coming down from sixteenths to triplets is the hard direction. Leave more room than feels right.
steps.payoff: The rhythm pyramid up and down in one take, and a riff that changes gear on every beat.

exercises.title: Two, three, four
exercises.purpose: One beat each of eighths, triplets and sixteenths, then a quarter note. Each beat has one more note than the last.
howTo: Count '1 and, 2-trip-let, 3 e and a, 4'.
Strict down-up from the first note. The quarter note on beat 4 is your check: it lands on the click or it doesn't.
exercises.coachLine: The quarter note on beat 4 tells me whether the three beats before it kept time. I'll say how even it was.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: The rhythm pyramid
exercises.purpose: One, two, three and four notes to a beat going up, then four, three, two and one coming down. Every division you have learned, in two bars.
howTo: Bar 1: a quarter, two eighths, a triplet, four sixteenths. Bar 2: the same rhythm in reverse.
The two beats of sixteenths meet at the bar line. Keep them the same speed on both sides of it.
exercises.coachLine: I'll say how even each beat was. The step down from four notes to three is where it usually drags.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: Three across two beats
exercises.purpose: Two quarter notes, then three notes spread evenly over the next two beats: the quarter-note triplet. Bar 2 turns it round, the triplet first. Slow, wide and easy to get wrong.
howTo: Count eighth-note triplets, '1-trip-let, 2-trip-let', and play every second syllable: '1, let, trip'.
The three notes are equal. If the last one is short, you fell back onto the beat too soon.
exercises.coachLine: I time the three notes against the triplet they are written on. I'll say how even they were.
selfCheck: Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: A riff that changes gear
exercises.purpose: A two-bar A minor pentatonic phrase at the fifth fret: eighths, a beat of sixteenths, a triplet and a landing note, then the gears in another order.
howTo: Bar 1: '1 and, 2 e and a, 3-trip-let, 4'. Bar 2: '1-trip-let, 2 e and a, 3 and, 4'.
Play it as a phrase, with the long notes as the places it is going to.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. I'll say how even it was and check the notes after the take.

steps.title: Rhythm on two strings at once
steps.goal: Play eighths, the long, short-short figure and a syncopated bar as a two-note power chord, and change between two chords in time.
steps.why: Until now every stroke has hit one string. A rhythm part is often more than one string at a time, and the smallest step in that direction is two: an open string and the note at fret 2 on the next string, which together make a power chord. The rhythms are ones you can already play. What is new is that the pick travels through two strings on the way down and the same two on the way up, and that both have to stop together in a rest.
howTo: The E power chord is the open low E string and fret 2 of the A string. The A power chord is the open A string and fret 2 of the D string. On other Takes there is a third, the D power chord: the open D string and fret 2 of the G string.

Until now the second finger played fret 2. For these chords use the first: it can lean lightly on the thinner strings beside it to keep them quiet, and it is the finger power chords use later. It hops one string across to change chord.
Aim the pick at the two strings of the chord only.
The hand swings as it always has: down on the beat, up on the 'and'. Each stroke is one short movement through both strings, so they sound as one.
In a rest, stop both strings at once: relax the first finger and lay the side of the picking hand on the strings.
steps.payoff: A four-bar riff on two power chords. From here, full chords are the First Chords and Strumming Path, and heavier riffs are the Metal Rhythm Path.

exercises.title: Two strings, down and up
exercises.purpose: The E power chord in quarter notes, then in eighths. Bar 1 is all downstrokes, to hear both strings; bar 2 adds the upstroke.
howTo: Bar 1: four quarter notes, all down, counted '1, 2, 3, 4'. Bar 2: six eighths, down-up, and a quarter note on beat 4: '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.
Every stroke is the same chord: the open low E string and fret 2 of the A string under the first finger.
Make the upstroke reach both strings. If only the A string sounds on the 'and', the stroke is too short.
exercises.coachLine: A chord counts as one stroke: timed and counted, and which notes were in it is not checked. The join between the bars is where the time usually slips.
selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord sound, and no others?

variants.label: A and D strings
variants.purpose: The A power chord in quarter notes, then in eighths. Bar 1 is all downstrokes, to hear both strings; bar 2 adds the upstroke.
howTo: Bar 1: four quarter notes, all down, counted '1, 2, 3, 4'. Bar 2: six eighths, down-up, and a quarter note on beat 4: '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.
Every stroke is the same chord: the open A string and fret 2 of the D string under the first finger.
Make the upstroke reach both strings. If only the D string sounds on the 'and', the stroke is too short.

variants.label: D and G strings
variants.purpose: The D power chord in quarter notes, then in eighths. Bar 1 is all downstrokes, to hear both strings; bar 2 adds the upstroke.
howTo: Bar 1: four quarter notes, all down, counted '1, 2, 3, 4'. Bar 2: six eighths, down-up, and a quarter note on beat 4: '1 and 2 and 3 and, 4'.
Every stroke is the same chord: the open D string and fret 2 of the G string under the first finger.

exercises.title: Long, short-short, at two speeds
exercises.purpose: The E power chord in the long, short-short rhythm: a quarter and two eighths in bar 1, then twice as fast in bar 2, an eighth and two sixteenths, the gallop figure.
howTo: Bar 1: count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and'. Down on each quarter note, down-up on the two eighths.
Bar 2: count '1, and a, 2, and a, 3, and a, 4'. Down, down-up on each of the first three beats, and one downstroke on beat 4.
Keep the strokes small in bar 2: the pick only has to clear two strings. The click does not change between the bars.
exercises.coachLine: A chord counts as one stroke: timed and counted, and which notes were in it is not checked. The first beat of bar 2 is where the time usually slips.

notes: At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord sound, and no others?

exercises.title: A syncopated bar on two strings
exercises.purpose: The syncopated rhythm from earlier in the Path as the E power chord: beats 2 and 3 are silent, and the chords around them fall on the 'and'.
howTo: Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and 4'. In bar 1 the chord on beat 4 is short, with a rest after it; in bar 2 it lasts the whole beat.
Stop both strings on every rest: relax the first finger and lay the side of the picking hand down. The hand keeps swinging in eighths and plays the air.
The chords on the 'and' are upstrokes. Tap the foot on the silent beats.
exercises.coachLine: Chords are timed and counted; which notes they were is not checked. A sound in a rest counts as an extra note; strings left humming are for your ear.
selfCheck: In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?
Did your foot keep tapping the beat through the off-beat notes?

exercises.title: A riff on two chords
exercises.purpose: Four bars on two power chords, a bar each and round again. Every bar ends on a chord that lasts a beat or more, so the hop comes after a long chord and never in the middle of a run.
howTo: Bars 1 and 2: count '1, 2 and, (3) and, 4'. Bar 3: '1 and, (2) and, (3) and, 4'. Bar 4: '1 and 2 and, 3, 4', the last chord struck on 3 and held through 4.
Bars 1 and 3 are the E power chord: the open low E string and fret 2 of the A string. Bars 2 and 4 are the A power chord: the open A string and fret 2 of the D string.
Hop the first finger across just before beat 1, not earlier: the chord before it should last its full length.
exercises.coachLine: This is the Step's test piece. The first chord of each bar, straight after the change, is the one that arrives late. Chords are timed and counted; which notes they were is not checked.
selfCheck: Did both strings of every chord sound, and no others?
In the rests, was the guitar silent, with no string left ringing?

steps.difficultyException: Fewer strokes a bar than the Step before, on purpose: every stroke is two strings, struck together and stopped together, which a note-rate metric does not count.

steps.title: With the band
steps.goal: Hold a riff in eighths, one in sixteenths and a shuffle against a real rhythm section, two to four bars at a time.
steps.why: A click tells you exactly where the beat is. A band tells you roughly, and gives you a feel to sit in. Locking a riff to a bass drum and a snare is the reason to practise rhythm at all, and it uses the ear differently from a click.
howTo: Listen to the bass drum and the snare, not to your own guitar. Your riff is one part of the groove.
If you get lost, stop, find beat 1 of the next bar and come back in there.
Use direct input or headphones for a graded take: the band reaching a microphone is something the app has not been tested against.
steps.payoff: Three riffs that sit inside a band: straight rock, sixteenth-note rock and a shuffle.

exercises.title: An eighth-note riff with the band
exercises.purpose: Four bars in E minor over a rock groove, with rests on beats 2 and 3 of the first three bars, where the drums speak. The riff follows the chords: E, G, A and back to E.
howTo: Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and 4 and' for three bars; bar 4 fills beat 3 and ends on a long note. The hand swings in eighths throughout.
The root is the note a chord is named after. Each bar starts on the root of its chord: open low E, G at fret 3, the open A string, and E again.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. I time your notes against it and check them after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A sixteenth-note riff with the band
exercises.purpose: Two bars on an E chord with the gallop on beat 1 and sixteenths with holes in them after it. The drums stay on eighths and you play inside them.
howTo: Bar 1: '1, and a, (2) e and, 3, and, 4 and'. Learn it at the first rung with the count.
Keep every note short and let the band fill the gaps.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. I'll say how even it was against the band and check the notes after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.
At this speed a real rig's input delay can push notes out of their matching window, which reads as late or missed. Evenness is the number to trust here, and only once the delay is calibrated.

exercises.title: A shuffle with the band
exercises.purpose: The boogie line over a blues shuffle: two bars on A, one on D, and home to A. The band swings, and your long-short has to swing with it.
howTo: The same shape as before on the A and D strings, then moved across to the D and G strings for the D chord.
Listen to the hi-hat or the ride: it plays the same long-short you do.
exercises.coachLine: Band on. I time your notes against the shuffle, so straight eighths will read as early.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

levels.title: Beginner: on the beat
levels.summary: Quarter notes, eighth notes and rests with a click, on the low strings and then higher up, and a first riff with a band: one note a beat, two notes a beat, and silence in time.

startHereIf: You've never practised with a click, or you find it hard to stay with one.
You can play a single note on an open string and at fret 3.
Eighth notes at 80 BPM are not yet steady for a whole bar.

warmups.title: A walk up one string
warmups.purpose: Long, short-short, long, short-short on two notes of a minor scale, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and'. First finger on the lower note, and move the hand up a note at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Start well under your clean tempo.
Pick both short notes of each pair.
Put each long note right on the click.
Wait for the click on each long note.
Count the long note's beat, then come in.
Move the hand up as each new bar starts.
Count '1, 2 and, 3, 4 and' to the last note.

warmups.title: Three notes and a rest
warmups.purpose: Three quarter notes and a beat of silence on two notes of a minor scale, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1, 2, 3, (4)' out loud and stop the string on 4. Move the hand up a note in the rest.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

cues.say: Count '1, 2, 3, (4)' out loud as you play.
Pick every written note, right to the end.
Play right on the click after each rest.
Count the rest out loud before you come in.
Move the hand up during the rest.
Stop the string on '4' right to the end.

levels.title: Intermediate: between the beats
levels.summary: Off-beats, dotted notes and the push, the sixteenth-note figures, and triplets with the shuffle.

startHereIf: You can play steady eighth notes with a click at 85 BPM, down on the beat and up on the 'and'.
You can stop for a beat and come back in on time.
A note on the 'and' with nothing on the beat before it throws you off.

warmups.title: The gallop up one string
warmups.purpose: Long-short-short on three notes of a minor scale and a quarter note to land on, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1, and a, 2, and a, 3, and a, 4' and move the hand up a note at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

warmups.title: Off-beats up one string
warmups.purpose: One note on the beat and then only the 'and' of every beat, on two notes of a minor scale, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1 and, (2) and, (3) and, (4) and', foot on every click. Move the hand up a note at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

levels.title: Advanced: changing gear
levels.summary: Sixteenths with rests in them, changes between eighths, triplets and sixteenths, two-string power chords, and riffs held against a band.

startHereIf: You can play the gallop figure, an eighth and two sixteenths, evenly at 70 BPM.
You can play eighth-note triplets at 80 BPM and a shuffle.
You speed up or slow down when the rhythm changes from one division to another, or you've never played with a band.

warmups.title: The pyramid up one string
warmups.purpose: A quarter, two eighths, a triplet and four sixteenths on three notes of a minor scale, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1, 2 and, 3-trip-let, 4 e and a' and move the hand up a note at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.

warmups.title: The skipping figure up one string
warmups.purpose: One, e, (and), a on each of three notes of a minor scale and a quarter note to land on, a step higher each bar. A different key and string each time.
howTo: Start well under your clean tempo. Count '1 e (and) a' on each beat: down, up, miss, up. Move the hand up a note at each bar line.
warmups.coachLine: This is a warm-up. It tells you how it went, and it decides nothing.
